label: This answer is a historical event
clue: This economic event happened on a single day in October 1929. On that day, the value of something millions of Americans had bought with their savings suddenly collapsed to almost nothing. Wealthy businessmen, everyday workers, and farmers who had borrowed money were all left with nothing overnight. This disaster happened in New York City and marked the beginning of the worst economic crisis in American history.

label: This answer is a word that describes a situation
clue: This was a condition that affected a huge number of American workers during the Great Depression. At the worst point, out of every four workers in America, one of them had no job at all. People who had once held steady jobs found themselves standing on street corners hoping for work. Families sold their possessions and moved in with relatives just to survive. The government set up offices where people in this condition could go to look for help.

label: This answer is a type of place or program
clue: These were a type of food program that appeared in American cities during the Great Depression. Charities and churches set them up so that people who had no money could still get a meal. A person would walk up, wait their turn, and receive a bowl of soup or a piece of bread for free. On any given day in the early 1930s, thousands of hungry people could be seen standing in these long lines on city streets. At their peak, some of these lines stretched for entire city blocks.

label: This answer is a historical event
clue: This economic crisis hit millions of American families in the early 1930s. People panicked and rushed to pull all their savings out of the bank at once. The banks ran out of money and had to close their doors forever. Families who had worked for decades to save money found that it had simply vanished overnight. President Roosevelt addressed this problem on his very first day in office by declaring a national "bank holiday."

label: This answer is a person
clue: This American president took office in 1933. He immediately began pushing dozens of new programs through Congress to help struggling Americans. He gave radio speeches called "fireside chats" to calm a frightened nation and explain his plans in simple language. His collection of government relief and reform programs became known as the New Deal.

label: This answer is a historical event
clue: This environmental disaster struck a large region of the United States throughout the 1930s. For many years, farmers had removed the deep-rooted grasses that held the soil in place. Then a long period without rain dried out the land completely. When powerful winds swept across the plains, they picked up the loose soil and carried it for hundreds of miles. Enormous black clouds of dirt rolled across states like Oklahoma, Texas, and Kansas, burying farms and suffocating livestock.

label: This answer is a word that describes a condition
clue: This natural condition played a major role in making the Great Depression even worse for farmers. Month after month passed with no rain, and the land began to crack and dry out. Without rain, crops withered and died in the fields. The dry soil had nothing holding it to the ground. When wind swept across the Great Plains, it picked up the loose soil and carried it hundreds of miles away. This condition, combined with years of poor farming, helped create the massive dust storms of the 1930s.

label: This answer is a word for a group of people
clue: This nickname was given to a group of families who fled their homes during the 1930s. Their farms in Oklahoma and surrounding states had been destroyed by drought and dust storms. They packed everything they owned into old cars and trucks and left with nowhere to go. They traveled a famous highway called Route 66, heading west toward California. They hoped to find work on farms in California, but were often met with hostility and turned away.

label: This answer is a type of place
clue: These were a type of settlement that appeared in American cities during the Great Depression. People who had lost their homes built them out of whatever scraps they could find — cardboard, tin, wood, and cloth. They were named mockingly after the president that many Americans blamed for the economic crisis. Large versions of these settlements appeared on the outskirts of cities like Los Angeles and Sacramento.

label: This answer is a historical event
clue: This is what historians call the massive movement of people from one part of the country to another during the 1930s. Drought, dust storms, and poverty pushed hundreds of thousands of families off their land in the Great Plains. Most of these families headed west, hoping that California's farms and warm climate meant there was work to be found. California's population grew dramatically during this period as a result of this movement of people.
